Lessons.Title: Function Notation
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: use notation f(a)=b to identify and communicate named input-output relationships, explain values in units and distinguish an input from the function's output. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 4 Lesson 2, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/4/2/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Publisher Addressing HSF-IF.A.1, HSF-IF.A.2 and HSF-IF.B.4. The source uses a dog's distance over time; this lesson retains context-sensitive interpretation with original data.

Original hiking example: a traveller's elevation above trailhead is represented by H(t)=20+15t metres for 0≤t≤4 hours. H(2)=50 means the traveller is 50 m above trailhead after two hours; it is not the number of hours nor a multiplication of H by 2. H(0)=20 describes an initial elevation of 20 metres.

Translate a verbal statement into f notation. If a reservoir has 280 litres after 3 hours, write V(3)=280 L, where V maps elapsed hours to remaining volume. A statement V(a)=V(b) means the two inputs yield the same measured volume; it does not force a=b for a non-injective function.

Student task: interpret at least five original notations with explicit units, map them to a labelled graph and table, explain why H(2) is different from 2H, and translate contextual data to notation in both directions. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for correctly named function and argument, accurate units, correct graph/table match and verbal interpretation.

V12 source-equivalent multi-function naming: the original source interprets three functions describing distance from a post over time, then introduces concise notation f(t),g(t),h(t). Use three independently invented probe models instead: f(t)=min(t,4) metres, g(t)=4−|t−3| metres, h(t)=2 metres for integer seconds t=0..6. At t=2, f(2)=2, g(2)=3, h(2)=2; at t=4, f(4)=4, g(4)=3, h(4)=2. Identical inputs can produce different outputs for DIFFERENT functions, without violating uniqueness within one named function. Source preparation/student: https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/4/2/preparation.html and https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/4/2/index.html.

V12 student task: match three original distance-time graphs to tables, name and use f, g and h, explain f(2)=2 metres in a sentence and compare it with g(2)=3 metres; translate one sentence into function notation and another back to the situation. Note the source expects interpretation from genuinely drawn graphs, so the existing one-function hiking calculation does not alone satisfy the activity.

Teacher draft rubric0–2 each for three correctly named function graph/table correspondences, input-output interpretation with units, meaning of multiple functions at same input, and student-authored notation/translation evidence.

KeyConcepts.Title: Function name
KeyConcepts.Definition: A symbol such as H represents a rule or relation giving an output for each permitted input.
KeyConcepts.Rule: H(t) denotes an output, not multiplication by a letter.

KeyConcepts.Title: Input argument
KeyConcepts.Definition: The quantity within parentheses is the input variable or value.
KeyConcepts.Example: In H(2), the input is 2 hours.

KeyConcepts.Title: Value statement
KeyConcepts.Definition: f(a)=b records the function's output b at input a.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Translate both directions between words and notation.
KeyConcepts.Example: V(3)=280 means volume after3 hours is280 litres.

WorkedExamples.Title: Evaluate notation in context
WorkedExamples.Question: Given H(t)=20+15t, find and interpret H(2).
WorkedExamples.Method: Represent the function with its stated input/output domain and verify the mathematical assertion.
Steps: Explain this represents elevation after 2 hours.

WorkedExamples.Title: Translate an observation to notation
WorkedExamples.Question: After three hours a reservoir holds 280 litres. Represent it using V.
WorkedExamples.Method: Represent the function with its stated input/output domain and verify the mathematical assertion.
Steps: Name function V as remaining volume in litres.
WorkedExamples.Check: The statement links an input and one output.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish f(a)=f(b) from equal inputs
WorkedExamples.Question: For F(t)=(t−2)², compare F(1) and F(3).
WorkedExamples.Method: Represent the function with its stated input/output domain and verify the mathematical assertion.
Steps: Outputs are equal despite inputs1 and3 being distinct.
Do not conclude input arguments must coincide.
WorkedExamples.Check: Function is not one-to-one across these inputs.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Function notation is evaluation, not an ordinary product.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Substitute the input into the named rule.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Many different inputs may share one output.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check if function is one-to-one before inferring equality of inputs.

SummaryPoints: f(a)=b identifies input a and output b of a named function.
Contextual notation must carry units for both quantities.
Different inputs may share the same output.
Graph matching and explanation are teacher-scored.

Visuals.Description: Independent original functional models and their exact numeric outputs, including domain limits.
